Abstract 33

Tissue damage and repair are hallmarks of the inflammatory process. Despite a wealth of 34

information on the mechanisms that govern tissue damage, mechanistic insight on how 35

inflammatory mediators affect repair is lacking. Here, we investigated how interferons influence 36

tissue repair after damage to the intestinal mucosa driven by inflammatory or physical injury. We 37

found that type III, but not type I or II, interferons delay epithelial cell regeneration by inducing the 38

upregulation of ZBP1, Caspase-8 activation, and cleavage of Gasdermin C (GSDMC). Cleaved 39

GSDMC drives epithelial cell death by pyroptosis and delays the re-epithelialization of the large 40

or small intestine after colitis or irradiation, respectively. We also found that the type III 41

interferon/ZBP1/Caspase-8/GSDMC pathway is activated in patients with inflammatory bowel 42

disease. Our findings highlight a molecular signaling cascade that affects the outcome of the 43

immune response by delaying tissue repair, which has important implications for human 44

inflammatory disorders. 45

INTRODUCTION. 46

The immune system has evolved to protect the host from external or internal threats, as 47

well as to maintain homeostasis of organs and tissues. The skin, lungs, gut, and other mucosae 48

are constantly exposed to microbial and/or physical perturbations and harbor multiple immune 49

and non-immune cells that sense the presence of hostile environmental or endogenous factors 50

and mount a defensive response. The causative agent of this response, the response itself, or 51

both, may lead to tissue damage. Tissue damage sensing by tissue-resident as well as newly 52

recruited cells initiates a complex cascade of cellular and molecular processes to restore tissue 53

functionality and homeostasis or adapt to persistent perturbations1. 54

The gastrointestinal tract represents an ideal tissue for exploring the mechanisms 55

underlying the exquisite balance between tissue damage and repair orchestrated by the immune 56

system. In the intestine, immune cells, epithelial cells, and commensal microbes are in a dynamic 57

equilibrium. A monolayer of highly specialized intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) separates the gut 58

lumen from the underlying lamina propria. The interplay between microbiota-derived inflammatory 59

cues and the host cells in the intestine profoundly affects the biology of the gut during 60

homeostasis, inflammation, and damage responses. The delicate equilibrium between the 61

microbiota, the epithelial barrier, and the immune system is lost during the development of 62

inflammatory bowel diseases (IBDs)2,3. IBDs are characterized by a heightened inflammatory 63

response, which is accompanied by a breach of the intestinal barrier that compromises mucosal 64

homeostasis. Understanding how immune mediators influence epithelial repair is fundamental for 65

identifying new strategies to promote mucosal healing4,5. 66

We previously showed that a group of interferons (IFNs), known as type III IFNs or IFN- 67

λ6-8, limits inflammation in a mouse model of colitis by dampening the tissue-damaging functions 68

of neutrophils9. IFN-λ, similarly to type I IFNs, plays potent anti-microbial roles 10. However, in 69

contrast to type I IFNs which act systemically because of the broad expression of the type I IFN 70

receptor (IFNAR), the expression of the IFN-λ receptor (IFNLR) is mainly restricted to epithelial 71

cells and neutrophils. The local activity of IFN-λ in mucosal tissues limits the extent of activation 72

of immune cells and is believed to prevent excessive tissue damage, while preserving the anti- 73

microbial functions of IFN-λ10. 74

Although we and others have shown that IFN-λ limits intestinal tissue damage9,11, the 75

involvement of this group of IFNs during tissue restitution in the gut is controversial. During 76

intestinal inflammation, IFN-λ and type I IFNs have been shown to function in a balanced and 77

compartmentalized manner to favor re-epithelization by inducing the secretion of epithelial growth 78

factors and acting, respectively, on IECs or immune cells resident in the lamina propria12. IFN-λ 79

has also been proposed to facilitate the proliferation of IECs via Signal Transducer and Activator 80

of Transcription 1 (STAT1) signaling13 and to partially enhance gut mucosal integrity during graft- 81

versus-host disease14. In contrast, artificial overexpression of IFN-λ in mice favored the death of 82

Paneth cells15, a group of cells that can facilitate IEC regeneration16,17. In keeping with a possible 83

detrimental role of IFN-λ during an inflammatory response at mucosal surfaces, we and others 84

have recently demonstrated that IFN-λ delays the proliferation of lung epithelial cells in murine 85

models of persistent viral infections18,19, as well as in the lower respiratory tract of COVID-19 86

patients with severe-to-critical outcomes20. Notably, IFN-λ and/or the IFNLR were found to be 87

upregulated in IBD patients13,15, but it is still debated whether this group of IFNs plays protective 88

or detrimental activities during intestinal inflammation. 89

Here, we dissected the role of IFN-λ during gut repair and found that IFN-λ initiates a 90

signaling pathway that delays epithelial cell regeneration, secondary to either colitis or radiation 91

damage in mice, and that is also activated in IBD patients. 92

RESULTS. 94

IFN-λ delays tissue repair during colitis. 95

To assess whether IFN-λ affects gut repair in mice during intestinal inflammation, we 96

utilized dextran sulfate sodium (DSS) to induce colitis. In this model, DSS is administered for 7 97

days in the drinking water and later removed to allow tissue repair (Figure 1A). We previously 98

showed that, during the first 7 days of acute inflammation upon DSS-administration, IFN-λ 99

signaling in neutrophils, but not in IECs, restrains intestinal damage9. The measurement of type 100

III IFN gene induction in DSS-treated mice revealed that the levels of IFN-λ, as well as Ifit1, an 101

interferon-stimulated gene (ISG), remain elevated after DSS removal (Figure S1A, B). These 102

data suggest that IFN-λ can play roles that go beyond the inflammatory phase of DSS-induced 103

colitis and can also affect the remission phase of colitis. 104

The repair phase of colitis is characterized by a profound remodeling of the intestinal 105

epithelial layer to allow tissue regeneration. To test the involvement of IFN-λ signaling in 106

controlling epithelial cell regeneration during the repair phase of colitis, we followed over time 107

colon length, tissue damage, and weight change in VilCREIfnlr1fl/fl mice, in which only IECs do not 108

respond to IFN-λ, compared to Ifnlr1fl/fl littermate controls. We found that the colons of mice of 109

both groups were shortened to the same extent at the peak of inflammation (day 8), demonstrating 110

that they were equally affected by DSS-induced acute inflammation, as we previously showed9 111

(Figure 1B). Conversely, mice with IECs that respond to IFN-λ showed a significant delay in the 112

recovery of colon length compared to VilCREIfnlr1fl/fl mice (Figure 1B). Of note, VilCREIfnlr1fl/fl mice 113

returned to a colon length that was similar to the one of untreated animals by Day 12 after DSS 114

administration, indicating a complete repair of their intestine (Figure 1B). Similar trends were 115

followed for tissue damage and weight loss (Figure 1C, S1C, D). Of note, gut repair in 116

MRP8CREIfnlr1fl/fl mice that lack IFN-λ signaling in neutrophils was not affected compared to Ifnlr1fl/fl 117

littermate controls, as assessed by colon length and weight change (Figure S1E, F). Overall, 118

these data demonstrate that endogenous IFN-λ signaling in IECs leads to delayed tissue repair 119

during DSS-induced colitis. 120

delays epithelial regeneration, we injected, or not, recombinant (r)IFN-λ in mice after DSS-induced 122

inflammation peaked (Figure 1A). We confirmed that rIFN-λ administration further upregulated 123

IFN-λ acts on IECs and delays tissue repair upon irradiation. 157

Our data in the DSS-induced colitis model demonstrated that IFN-λ acts on IECs to delay 158

repair. To obtain mechanistic insights into the activity of IFN-λ on IECs, we employed a well- 159

characterized model of epithelial damage resulting from exposure to ionizing radiation 24 (Figure 160

1J). The repair of the gut epithelial monolayer is a complex process, and the regenerative capacity 161

of intestinal stem cells (ISCs) plays a critical role25. After targeted irradiation, ISC death in the 162

small intestine is followed by the repair of the damaged epithelial crypts and the return to 163

homeostasis. 164

We initially tested whether IFN-λ was induced upon irradiation and found that the levels of 165

type III IFNs increase over time peaking at 48-72 hours (h) after radiation injury (Figure S1P). We 166

next assessed crypt regeneration in WT mice, WT mice administered exogenous rIFN-λ, or Ifnlr1- 167

/- mice 96h after radiation injury, during the peak of the repair response. WT and Ifnlr1-/- mice were 168

co-housed prior to irradiation. We found that mice that received rIFN-λ showed reduced 169

regeneration of the crypts, while Ifnlr1-/- mice had an increased number of crypts (Figure 1K). Of 170

note, while the number of crypts 1 day post irradiation was similar in WT and Ifnlr1-/- mice, 3 days 171

after challenge WT mice showed a significant delay in repair compared to Ifnlr1-/- mice (Figure 172

1L). Irradiated WT and Ifnlr1-/- mice, administered or not rIFN-λ, revealed that both exogenous 173

and endogenous IFN-λ signaling impairs crypt regeneration (Figure S1Q, R). Notably, 174

endogenous IFN-λ, but not type I IFN, signaling caused the delay in tissue repair (Figure 1M). 175

IFN-λ-dependent activation of Gasdermin C (GSDMC) delays intestinal repair upon irradiation- or 259

colitis-driven damage. 260

To determine the molecular mechanisms regulated by IFN-λ to dampen tissue restitution, 261

we identified the genes differentially regulated in epithelial cells derived from irradiated WT, 262

compared to VilCREIfnlr1fl/fl, mice (Figure 2C). We found that Zbp1, an important regulator of cell 263

fate that has been shown to govern pyroptosis, apoptosis, as well as necroptosis34,35, was among 264

the ISGs significantly upregulated by endogenous IFN-λ in IECs in response to irradiation (Figure 265

2C). We also found that protein levels of ZBP1 were upregulated in epithelial cells of the small 266

intestine upon in vivo administration of rIFN-λ in non-irradiated WT, but not VilCREIfnlr1fl/fl, mice 267

(Figure S4A). Upregulation of these proteins was not different in the absence of rIFN-λ in the two 268

backgrounds (Figure S4A). 269

Among other genes significantly upregulated only in cells that respond to IFN-λ, there 270

were two members of the GSDMC family, Gsdmc2 and Gsdmc3. GSDMs are critical effectors of 271

pyroptosis, a form of inflammatory cell death36,37, and their involvement in gastrointestinal 272

pathophysiology has recently gained attention38. The GSDMC family, in particular, is composed 273

of GSDMC1-4 in mice, and by GSDMC in humans. Some reports have involved GSDMCs in the 274

lytic death of tumor cells39,40, or of enterocytes during helminth infections41,42, but very little is 275

known about the activity of GSDMCs during colitis. We confirmed previous work41,42 and found 276

that GSDMCs were expressed exclusively along the intestinal tract, both in the small and large 277

intestine (Figure S4B). qPCR analyses of Gsdmc1-4 confirmed expression along the 278

GSDMC was present in IECs, but not in the lamina propria (Figure S4D). Of note, resting mice 280

additional pathways that follow irradiation-induced damage regulate Gsdmc gene expression 282

and/or protein synthesis. We then assessed the expression of GSDMCs in the different clusters 283

identified in our scRNAseq analyses and found that Gsdmc2, Gsdmc3 and Gsdmc4 are 284

2L, Figure S3B). Consistently with GSDMCs expression, these populations are the one mostly 286

contributing to the differences in frequencies between WT and VilCREIfnlr1fl/fl populations. 287

when constitutively expressed, and/or induced, in HEK293T cells (Figure 3A, B, S4E). 292

DISCUSSION. 577

In our work, we revealed that IFN-λ restrains the regeneration of the epithelial barrier either 578

during colitis or secondary to ionizing radiation toxicity. Overall, our data support a model in which 579

IFN-λ is necessary to prime IECs by upregulating ZBP1 and GSDMCs. ZBP1 then functions as 580

the sensor of tissue damage by recognizing Z-NAs, allowing the formation of a cell death complex 581

that contains ZBP1, RIPKs, ASC, Casp-8, as well as GSDMCs. ZBP1 activation in response to 582

Z-NAs leads to the activation of Casp-8 and, consequently, to the cleavage of GSDMCs that 583

execute pyroptotic cell death and delay gut repair. We also found that biopsies derived from both 584

UC and CD patients present, compared to healthy individuals, elevated levels of ZBP1 and active 585

Casp-8 and GSDMC. We also identified increased levels of distinct members of the type III IFN 586

25

family or a significant correlation between type III IFNs and ZBP1 and cleaved Casp-8 and 587

GSDMC in UC and CD patients, respectively. Our single cell analyses demonstrated that, in mice, 588

induction of epithelial cell death via the ZBP1-GSDMC axis reduces the number of ISCs, thus 589

affecting the re-epithelization of the injured intestine. Finally, we revealed that IFN-λ, but not type 590

I or type II IFNs, are the major drivers of the delayed repair of the damaged gut, opening new 591

ways of therapeutic intervention for individuals that encounter tissue damage such as IBD patients 592

or subjects exposed to radiation therapies. 593

We and others previously described the capacity of IFN-λ to dampen lung epithelial cell 594

proliferation and to drive their apoptosis18,19. Similar anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic 595

transcriptional programs were found in the lung of patients with severe-to-critical COVID-1920. Of 596

note, our new data reveal the absence of expression of GSMDC in the lung at the protein or 597

mRNA levels. These findings are in agreement with our previous RNAseq data that did not identify 598

Gsdmc2,3 as genes upregulated in the lung epithelial cell of mice exposed to virus ligands that 599

induce IFN-λ production18. Regardless of the modality of cell death induced by IFN-λ in different 600

organs, another important observation we made refers to the differential regulation of distinct 601

members of the type III IFN family in driving inflammatory pathologies in humans. Our previous 602

investigation of COVID-19 patients identified IFN-λ1 as a protective IFN produced in the upper 603

airways upon SARS-CoV-2 encounter. In contrast, IFN-λ2/-λ3 were highly upregulated both in the 604

lower and upper airways of patients with severe-to-critical COVID-19. In our work, we now 605

demonstrate that UC patients present high protein levels of IFN-λ2/-λ3, but not of IFN-λ1. 606

Similarly, CD patients show a strong correlation between the protein levels of IFN-λ2/-λ3, but not 607

of IFN-λ1 or other IFNs, and the levels of ZBP1, as well as activated Casp-8 and GSDMC. Future 608

immune cells during recovery from intestinal injury. 666

Another critical aspect highlighted by our findings is that the cells targeted by IFN-λ die by 667

pyroptosis as a consequence of GSDMC cleavage. ZBP1 can interact directly or indirectly with 668

proteins that regulate cell death and drive the activation of apoptotic caspases, the necroptosis 669

effector MLKL, or pyroptosis effectors Casp-1, 11 and GSDMD35,37,46,47. Several works reported 670

the capacity of ZBP1-containing cell death complexes, known as PANoptosomes, to 671

simultaneously drive in macrophages the activation of multiple forms of cell death, in a process 672

called PANoptosis46,57-59. Of note, the presence of ASC is a characteristic of multiple 673

PANoptosomes, and we found that ASC is also required to drive the death of IECs downstream 674

of IFN-λ. Another key feature of the PANoptosomes is that all the forms of cell death involved 675

need to be concomitantly blocked to prevent the death of the cells. In the case of IECs, we found 676

that only blockade of GSDMCs, but not the absence of the necroptosis-executor MLKL or 677

inhibition of GSDMD activation, prevents the death of IECs in the organoid models. In keeping 678

with our in vitro data, we also excluded in vivo that GSDMD or GSDME play roles similar to 679

GSDMC. These data, together with our finding that in vivo inhibition of Casp-8, as well as 680

GSDMC-deficiency, mimic the lack of IFN-λ signaling,  highlight the essential role played by the 681

ZBP1/Casp-8/GSDMC axis in driving cell death in IECs via GSDMC-dependent pyroptosis, 682

compared to other executors of cell death. It will be important to test in the future how tissue 683

and/or cell type specific cell death complexes differentially orchestrate distinct types of cell death. 684

Overall, our data unveiled a new axis between IFN-λ, ZBP1, Casp-8, and GSDMC that 685

governs mucosal repair in the gut and opens new perspectives to future therapeutic interventions. 686

Limitations of the study. 688


<!-- Page 30 -->


29

Our work revealed a new pathway that leads to cell death in IECs delaying gut repair. We 689

demonstrated that IFN-λ drives the upregulation of ZBP1 and GSDMC, and allows the formation 690

of a cell death complex that, upon recognition of Z-NAs, drives the activation of Casp-8 and 691

GSDMCs, to induce pyroptotic cell death of ISCs. Of note, resting mice treated with rIFN-λ did 692

not show upregulation of GSDMCs, demonstrating that additional signals that follow irradiation- 693

or colitis-induced damage regulate Gsdmc gene expression and/or protein synthesis. The nature 694

of these signals, as well as the nature of the stimuli that regulate IFN-λ induction, have not been 695

investigated in this study. An intriguing hypothesis is that Z-NAs may serve not only as the 696

activating stimulus for the cell death complex, but also to drive IFN-λ and/or the expression of 697

GSDMCs, but future investigations will be needed to prove or disprove this possibility. 698

A limitation of the data obtained in human individuals relates to the fact that we could not 699

distinguish the tissue damaging phase from the remission phase in our patients. In humans, it is 700

almost impossible to determine the exact phase of IBD because both tissue damage and repair 701

can be simultaneous and/or can be happening in distinct areas of the gut. This is particularly true 702

for CD, and indeed the levels of all IFNs measured in CD patients didn’t show major statistical 703

differences compared to HCs. 704

Another limitation of our study also relates to the human samples utilized. Although we 705

found highest level of IFN-λ2/-λ3 in UC patients, low, but statistically significant, levels of IFN-α2 706

were also detected. On the other hand, as stated above, none of the IFN tested reached statistical 707

significance in terms of upregulation in CD patients compared to HCs (although the level of IFN- 708

λ2/-λ3, but not other IFNs, was significantly associated to ZBP1, Casp-8, and GSDMC). To 709

unequivocally identify the exact nature of the IFN(s) associated to the activation of the 710

ZBP1/Casp-8/GSDMC axis in IBD, patients should be sampled longitudinally and possibly at 711

multiple inflammatory and non-inflammatory sites, and a broader analysis of all the members of 712

the three IFN families should be performed. 713


<!-- Page 31 -->


30

Regardless of these limitations, our findings identified a new pathway that can be 714

pharmacologically targeted in the future to ameliorate tissue repair of the intestine under multiple 715

inflammatory conditions. 716
